name: Strawberry GraphQL
vendor: Strawberry GraphQL contributors (created by Patrick Arminio)
summary: A code-first Python GraphQL library: you write dataclass-style classes with type hints, and Strawberry turns them into the schema.
intro: Strawberry builds the schema from ordinary Python type hints, in the style of `dataclasses`. You decorate a class with `@strawberry.type`, and each annotated attribute becomes a field: `title: str` becomes `title: String!`, and `str | None` becomes a nullable `String`. A method marked `@strawberry.field` is a resolver, and its return annotation is the field’s type. `strawberry.Schema(query=Query)` turns those classes into a GraphQL-core schema, and printing it shows the SDL. Because the classes are the schema, the same classes serve as the data objects your resolvers return, and a mypy plugin type-checks them like any other Python code. The FastAPI documentation recommends Strawberry because it’s built on type annotations, as FastAPI is.

Strawberry ships its own integrations: a `GraphQLRouter` for FastAPI (an `APIRouter` whose context getter is a FastAPI dependency), plus views for Django, Flask, Quart, AIOHTTP, Channels and plain ASGI. Subscriptions work over WebSockets, and optionally SSE or multipart. It includes a DataLoader for batching, permission classes, Relay helpers and Apollo Federation, and has experimental `@defer` and `@stream` support, which needs GraphQL-core 3.3. It is still on 0.x version numbers (0.332.0 on October 6, 2026) and releases often; its breaking-changes page lists 20 releases with breaking changes since December 2022.
strengths: One source of truth: the type hints are the schema, the data classes and what mypy checks
First-party integrations, including a FastAPI router that supports FastAPI dependencies for the context
Tracks GraphQL-core closely: it requires 3.3 and offers experimental `@defer` and `@stream`
Built-in DataLoader, permission classes, Relay and Apollo Federation support
limits: Still 0.x with frequent releases: 20 releases with breaking changes since December 2022, so upgrades need reading the notes
Sync resolvers run on the event loop, so under FastAPI one slow `def` resolver blocks the whole worker; the docs recommend `async def` everywhere
The DataLoader and `@defer`/`@stream` work only with async execution; `execute_sync` and the sync views return an error for incremental delivery
Code first only: the Python classes are the source of truth, so a schema designed in SDL is converted once (`strawberry schema-codegen`) and then maintained as Python

story: Until 2018, Python had one main GraphQL library, Graphene, which defines fields with its own type classes. Patrick Arminio, a backend engineer in London, had contributed to Graphene, but decided to “make something else just to scratch my own itch”. Python 3.7 had added `dataclasses`, which turn annotated class attributes into fields, and Arminio used the same idea for GraphQL types: the repository started in December 2018, and version 0.1.0 reached PyPI in March 2019.

At PyCon DE 2019 Arminio presented it as “a dataclasses inspired approach to GraphQL”, eight months into the work. A mypy plugin (September 2019) made the schema type-checkable, a Django view followed the same month, then Apollo Federation (2020), a built-in DataLoader and Pydantic models (November 2020), and a FastAPI router (October 2021). The FastAPI documentation now recommends it as the GraphQL library closest to FastAPI’s own design.

Strawberry has stayed on 0.x versions and kept close to GraphQL-core: it added experimental `@defer` and `@stream` in July 2025 against GraphQL-core’s 3.3 pre-releases, and in September 2026 required GraphQL-core 3.3.0, dropping 3.2.

choices.choice: Dataclass-style classes instead of field objects
choices.why: Python 3.7’s `dataclasses` already turned annotated attributes into fields. Reusing that pattern means a GraphQL type reads like any other Python data class, and the classes double as the objects resolvers return.
With the types in annotations rather than in library-specific field classes, standard tools can check them: a mypy plugin type-checks Strawberry types like the rest of the code.

choices.choice: Permission classes borrowed from Django REST framework
choices.why: Arminio wanted fields that stay generic but don’t return data to the wrong people, so a field takes a list of permission classes, as views do in Django REST framework.
